question: Can feature learning in two-layer networks at vanishing initialization be represented by an alternating process that predicts which dormant unit activates, when it activates, and which loss plateau follows, while unifying known linear cases and explaining sequential Fourier-feature acquisition in modular addition?

key_findings.claim: Alternating Gradient Flows models a staircase training trajectory as repeated utility maximization by dormant neurons followed by loss minimization by active neurons.
key_findings.evidence: At each round, dormant units independently follow a projected flow of their correlation with the active-set residual, while an accumulated-utility clock determines the first activation. Active units then jointly follow gradient flow to a restricted critical point, the residual is recomputed, and the process repeats until no useful dormant unit or no gradient remains.

key_findings.claim: The general AGF ansatz is motivated by, but does not bound, an approximation that drops interactions among dormant neurons and treats active neurons as equilibrated.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B decomposes a dormant neuron's exact gradient into its utility against the active residual and a second term involving every dormant neuron, then declares the latter negligible when dormant norms are small. The authors identify a Hartman-Grobman-style argument as a possible route to rigor rather than supplying an error estimate or a general convergence theorem.

key_findings.claim: Homogeneity yields an accumulated-utility activation clock whose scale differs qualitatively between quadratic-in-parameters and higher-order neurons.
key_findings.evidence: For a leading homogeneous degree κ, the norm is exponential in accumulated utility when κ=2 and a power law when κ>2. Equations 16-17 give exact threshold expressions under the approximate dormant dynamics and lower bounds from maximal utility; the threshold is defined by the convention that a unit becomes active at norm greater than one.

key_findings.claim: Instantaneous directional alignment in accelerated vanishing-initialization time is justified only for κ=2, even though the attention and quadratic modular-addition applications have κ=3.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem B.2 shows that the accelerated angular-speed factor diverges only for κ=2 and tends to one for κ>2. The transformer and modular-addition sections explicitly assume instantaneous alignment to obtain jump-time lower bounds, while Appendix B.5 proposes a neuron-specific adaptive learning rate that would restore it but is not the optimizer analyzed in those applications.

key_findings.claim: For diagonal linear networks under the paper's initialization and data assumptions, AGF converges pointwise to the same limiting saddle sequence and jump times as the established Pesme-Flammarion characterization of gradient flow.
key_findings.evidence: Utility maximization has an explicit Riccati solution and accumulated-utility formula; cost minimization is a sign-constrained least-squares problem. Theorem 3.1 identifies the α→0 limit with the Pesme-Flammarion recursive algorithm, using learning-rate time rescaling proportional to minus log α and the asymptotics of log cosh.

key_findings.claim: AGF permits an activated neuron to return to dormancy, so its active-set path need not be monotone.
key_findings.evidence: A conserved imbalance quantity gives a lower bound on unit norm but vanishes with balanced small initialization, allowing an active unit to approach the origin. The diagonal two-coordinate example shows the first coordinate's accumulated utility returning to zero, flipping sign, and later reactivating.

key_findings.claim: For fully connected two-layer linear networks, AGF recovers greedy low-rank learning, but the advertised noncommuting-covariance trajectory is a conjecture rather than a general theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Because hidden-neuron identities are noncanonical under GL(H) symmetry, the analysis switches to orthogonal singular basis vectors. Utility selects singular modes and cost solves reduced-rank regression, matching Greedy Low-Rank Learning. Exact jump ordering is proved when the input covariance commutes with the task covariance; for the general case, singular-vector rotation leaves Conjecture 4.1 open despite Figure 4 agreement.

key_findings.claim: In the paper's rank-one attention-only linear-transformer setting, AGF reproduces sequential principal-component regression and exact post-activation loss levels, while its activation-time statement is only a lower bound.
key_findings.evidence: The kth dormant head's utility is a Rayleigh quotient whose maximizer aligns key and query with the kth unused eigenvector of input covariance. Orthogonality decouples active-head losses and fixes the learned component magnitude. Equation 7 and Appendix E.3 give the prediction and loss sequence, but the jump time uses maximal utility and assumed instantaneous alignment for κ=3.

key_findings.claim: For centered modular addition with the stated Fourier-separation assumptions, the initial utility has no non-global local maxima and is maximized by a neuron aligned to the largest-magnitude remaining harmonic.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5.1 expresses the utility in Fourier coordinates and characterizes all unit-sphere maximizers as phase-compatible cosine waves at the dominant frequency. The updated residual removes that conjugate frequency pair, so the argument recursively orders subsequent features by decreasing Fourier coefficient magnitude.

key_findings.claim: The modular-addition cost analysis characterizes a restricted synchronized regime, not unconstrained gradient flow for the original one-neuron-at-a-time AGF algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: The proof assumes a group of N neurons activates simultaneously although Algorithm 1 activates one neuron per round, requires N at least six to attain the loss lower bound, and assumes aligned neurons remain in one harmonic. The paper identifies resonant escape directions unless square terms cancel through coordinated amplitudes and phases. Thus the Fourier sequence is a strong mechanism result under explicit conditions, but not a general convergence proof for arbitrary training trajectories.

key_findings.claim: The headline modular-addition illustration lies outside the paper's stated odd-modulus proof assumption.
key_findings.evidence: The setup assumes p odd to avoid the Nyquist frequency, and the appendix proof uses odd p to assert that 2ξ and 4ξ are nonzero modulo p. Figure 6 instead uses p=20 with frequencies 1, 3, and 5; in particular 4 times 5 is zero modulo 20. The visual match can remain empirical, but it is not a direct in-assumption validation of the stated theorem chain.

key_findings.claim: The empirical support is visually persuasive in selected toy systems but is not a quantitative approximation study.
key_findings.evidence: Figures compare gradient descent curves or learned modes with numerical AGF predictions in a diagonal network, constructed linear regression, linear attention, and a sparse-spectrum modular task. The paper reports no trajectory distance, jump-time error table, confidence intervals, number of random seeds, failure rate, or held-out model-selection protocol for these matches.

key_findings.claim: Width can turn discrete-looking feature acquisitions into overlapping transitions that AGF no longer tracks closely.
key_findings.evidence: On a subset of CIFAR-10 with a two-layer ReLU network, Figure 7 shows staircase-like narrow-network loss curves becoming a smooth slide as width increases. The paper explains that several dormant units cross their thresholds in close succession and their cost phases overlap, weakening correspondence with sequential AGF.

key_findings.claim: AGF's formal notion of a feature is architecture-dependent and narrower than a general mechanistic-interpretability feature theory.
key_findings.evidence: The related-work appendix contrasts human-interpretable activation directions, circuits, and motifs with the deep-learning-theory definition based on neural-tangent-kernel change. The paper says it implicitly adopts the latter while studying mechanistic-interpretability tasks; concrete features are then coordinates, singular modes, principal components, or Fourier harmonics depending on the model.

anchors.section: Appendix A.1, What is a feature?

method.core_idea: Approximate small-initialization gradient flow by explicitly separating slow dormant-unit alignment and growth from rapid active-set refitting, making each feature acquisition an activation event with a predicted direction, time, and loss plateau.
method.mechanism: For an origin-passing two-layer unit, AGF defines utility as correlation between that unit's output and the residual produced by active units. Near a saddle, it drops dormant-dormant interactions, decomposes each dormant update into angular and radial dynamics, and integrates normalized utility until one norm crosses an active threshold. It then holds dormant units aside while active units minimize the restricted loss, permits collapsed units to return to dormancy, recomputes the residual, and iterates. Architecture-specific symmetry, spectral, or Fourier structure makes the two subproblems explicit in diagonal linear, fully connected linear, linear-attention, and modular-addition examples.
assumptions: The base model is a two-layer network with an origin-passing activation and mean-squared loss under continuous-time gradient flow.
Initialization scale tends to zero, and time or learning rate is rescaled so long saddle plateaus remain visible in the limit.
Near each saddle, active neurons are at a restricted local minimum and dormant neurons are sufficiently small that their mutual residual contribution is negligible.
The activation is homogeneous, or its utility has a usable leading homogeneous Taylor term of degree κ near the origin.
A unit becomes active when its norm reaches the conventional O(1) threshold represented as one; conclusions about absolute jump times inherit that convention.
Utility projected gradient flow reaches the relevant maximizing direction; general nonconvex utility landscapes and tied maxima are not resolved by the framework.
Cost minimization converges to the selected restricted critical point before another activation materially changes the residual.
Only the diagonal linear setting has a complete AGF-to-gradient-flow convergence proof; other applications add symmetry, spectral, rank, or harmonic assumptions.
The fully connected linear conjecture needs ordering through changing singular-vector bases and is proved only under a commutativity condition.
The rank-one attention analysis uses Gaussian inputs, linear regression in context, a special zero/small initialization, and κ=3 heads.

The modular-addition proof assumes centered encodings, odd modulus, distinct magnitudes for nonconjugate Fourier coefficients, sufficient hidden units, grouped activation, and preserved harmonic alignment with cancellation of resonant square terms.
Numerical AGF can stand in for exact subproblem solutions in plots, even though computational cost and sensitivity are not analyzed.

techniques.role: Represents a saddle by zero-scale dormant units and equilibrated active units.
Scores a dormant unit by its output correlation with what the active network has not yet fit.
Separates fast angular alignment from slower norm growth near small initialization.
Integrates normalized utility to predict which unit reaches activation scale first and when.
Maps each loss drop to refitting the currently active feature set.
Allows a feature coefficient to return through zero, leave the active set, change sign, and later reactivate.
Uses κ to determine norm dynamics, time rescaling, and whether instantaneous alignment is asymptotically justified.
Replaces noncanonical hidden neurons in a linear factorization with orthogonal rank-one singular basis vectors.
Alternates top residual singular-mode selection with reduced-rank regression.
Interprets rank-one attention heads as cubic neurons that sequentially add unused covariance eigenvectors.
Uses cyclic symmetry and the discrete Fourier transform to identify utility-maximizing modular-addition features.
Shows that a fitted conjugate frequency pair disappears from the next dormant-unit utility.
Proposes a norm-dependent learning rate that would restore fast angular alignment for κ greater than two, without using it in the principal applications.

evaluations.setting: Two-dimensional diagonal linear regression from initialization u=square-root(2)α and v=0 across decreasing α.
evaluations.metric: Visual agreement of loss plateaus, coefficient path, parameter path, accumulated utility, angles, and jump times.
evaluations.result: Gradient flow approaches the AGF/Pesme-Flammarion piecewise-constant saddle sequence and includes a coordinate that collapses, flips sign, and reactivates.
evaluations.baseline: Exact gradient flow at several finite initialization scales.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer fully connected linear regression with Gaussian inputs, power-law input covariance, and a random target map, under commuting and noncommuting covariance cases.
evaluations.metric: Singular-value trajectories and predicted jump locations.
evaluations.result: The dashed AGF/conjecture curves visually track gradient-flow singular values in both displayed cases; only the commuting case is covered by the complete derivation.

evaluations.setting: Rank-one multi-head linear attention trained for Gaussian in-context linear regression.
evaluations.metric: Evolution of singular values of the learned attention map, analytic component magnitudes, and jump-time lower bounds.
evaluations.result: Heads visually add principal components in the predicted order and approach the analytic magnitudes; numerical AGF is described as an excellent approximation without a tabulated error.
evaluations.baseline: Direct gradient-flow simulation and the prior scalar-ODE analysis of the same model.

evaluations.setting: Quadratic two-layer network on modular addition with p=20, H=18, and an encoding composed of Fourier magnitudes 10, 5, and 2.5 at frequencies 1, 3, and 5.
evaluations.metric: Output power spectrum, reconstructed templates, learned-neuron spectra/phases, and numerical AGF trajectory.
evaluations.result: The three frequencies appear sequentially in decreasing magnitude and groups of neurons distribute phases as predicted; the experiment is outside the stated odd-p proof assumption.
evaluations.baseline: Direct gradient-descent training from the same initialization.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer ReLU network on a subset of CIFAR-10 under extremely small initialization while varying hidden width.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative loss-curve shape and correspondence between numerical AGF and gradient descent.
evaluations.result: Narrow networks show trackable steps; wider networks show overlapping activations, smoother loss, and weaker AGF agreement.
evaluations.baseline: Gradient descent versus numerical AGF at each width.

limitations: Author-stated: general convergence of AGF to gradient flow in the vanishing-initialization limit remains open and may fail.
Author-stated: empirical validation of the limit requires both initialization scale and learning rate to approach zero, making it difficult.
Author-stated: natural-data loss curves are often not visibly stepwise, and overlapping activation/cost phases weaken the sequential model.
Author-stated: population-level transitions in teacher-student and multi-index models are not represented by individual dormant-unit activation.
Author-stated: the framework is limited to two-layer networks; extension to deeper realistic architectures is open.
Reviewer-identified: dropping dormant-dormant interactions is the central approximation, yet no finite-initialization error bound controls the accumulated effect over long plateaus.
Reviewer-identified: finding a utility maximizer and a restricted local minimum can itself be a difficult nonconvex optimization problem, so AGF is not generally a cheaper predictive algorithm.
Reviewer-identified: activation at norm one is a modeling convention and jump times may not be invariant to architecture-specific scale or parametrization.
Reviewer-identified: instantaneous alignment fails asymptotically for κ greater than two under the base optimizer, narrowing the attention and modular jump-time claims.
Reviewer-identified: the fully connected noncommuting result is Conjecture 4.1 supported by a plot, not a theorem.
Reviewer-identified: the modular cost proof replaces one-at-a-time activation with simultaneous groups of at least six and assumes harmonic preservation plus resonance cancellation.
Reviewer-identified: the modular experiment uses even p=20 despite an odd-p theorem assumption and includes frequency 5, for which the proof's 4ξ nonresonance condition fails.
Reviewer-identified: empirical comparisons are qualitative and provide no seed counts, approximation errors, confidence intervals, or failure rates.
Reviewer-identified: the analysis is gradient-flow based and does not characterize minibatch SGD noise, momentum, adaptive optimization, finite steps, or regularization.
failure_modes: Many dormant units can reach threshold within one cost-relaxation time, merging discrete feature acquisitions into a smooth collective transition.
At finite initialization, dormant units can contribute enough to the residual that their supposedly independent utility flows interact and reorder activations.
Repeated singular values, equal Fourier magnitudes, or other symmetries can create ties and rotations that remove a unique next feature.
For κ greater than two, slow angular dynamics can cause a unit to grow before reaching the globally best utility direction.
Utility projected flow can settle at a nonglobal local maximum in architectures lacking the paper's Rayleigh-quotient or Fourier structure.
Active-set cost flow can converge to an unintended restricted local minimum or fail to equilibrate before another unit becomes influential.
A unit can collapse and reactivate with a different sign, making naive monotone feature-count interpretations wrong.
Stochastic gradient noise can perturb escape directions and jump-time ordering, especially across nearly tied utilities.
Deep networks have layer-coupled symmetries and conservation laws that do not admit an independent two-layer neuron partition.
Resonant Fourier frequencies can generate gradients outside the assumed harmonic subspace and invalidate recursive deflation.
On realistic wide networks, population-level representation changes can occur without an identifiable single unit crossing an O(1) norm threshold.
Numerical AGF can be as expensive or initialization-sensitive as the original training when both utility and cost phases require long inner flows.
reusable_insights: Residual correlation can serve as an architecture-specific definition of which dormant feature is most useful next.
Separating angular alignment from radial growth exposes which initialization and homogeneity regimes support clean stagewise learning.
An integrated local-growth rate provides a more informative activation clock than an instantaneous gradient or Hessian eigenvalue alone.
Feature selection and coefficient refitting form a common template linking neural dynamics to sparse regression, low-rank pursuit, PCA, and Fourier deflation.
Symmetry can make literal neurons noncanonical; choosing invariant basis elements avoids attributing features to arbitrary hidden-unit coordinates.
The homogeneity order κ is a falsification diagnostic: if it does not yield fast alignment, stagewise arguments must model angular and radial motion jointly.
Allowing active features to collapse prevents an unjustified monotone-support assumption and connects neural paths to signed active-set methods.
A residual update that exactly removes one orthogonal mode makes sequential learning analytically tractable and suggests controlled synthetic benchmarks.
Wide-network smoothing can arise from superposed sharp transitions, so a smooth aggregate loss does not alone disprove discrete microscopic acquisitions.
Every apparent unifying ansatz should be audited separately for approximation error, subproblem solvability, tie handling, and overlap between timescales.
open_questions: Under what minimal conditions does the full gradient-flow trajectory converge to AGF beyond diagonal linear networks?
Can one bound the neglected dormant-dormant term over the initialization-dependent plateau duration?
How should AGF be generalized when multiple neurons activate within the same asymptotic timescale?
Can coupled angular-radial dynamics replace the instantaneous-alignment approximation for κ greater than two and yield accurate jump times?
What determines the correct activation threshold in scale-invariant or normalized architectures?
Can the noncommuting fully connected linear conjecture be proved while tracking rotations of residual singular vectors?
Does the modular Fourier sequence hold under the actual one-neuron-at-a-time dynamics without grouped activation and imposed harmonic preservation?
How do even moduli, Nyquist modes, repeated Fourier magnitudes, non-Abelian groups, and multiple summands change the feature sequence?
How do minibatch noise, label noise, momentum, Adam, weight decay, and finite learning rates alter escape direction and activation ordering?
Can activation events be detected robustly in large realistic networks through invariant subspaces rather than individual neuron norms?
What quantitative trajectory metric should be used to compare AGF and training across initialization, width, depth, and data complexity?
Can AGF predict generalization or transfer consequences of feature order, not only training-loss drops?
Is there a computationally efficient approximate AGF whose subproblems are cheaper than simulating the original network?
How should feature identity be defined when several neurons collectively implement one circuit or a distributed representation?

competitive_landscape.title: Saddle-to-Saddle Dynamics in Diagonal Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Pesme and Flammarion already fully characterize the vanishing-initialization diagonal-linear gradient-flow path, including visited saddles, jump times, nonmonotone support, and the minimum-l1 endpoint. AGF's diagonal theorem proves that its generic utility/cost language reduces to this algorithm; the new value is unification and transfer, not a stronger result in the diagonal setting.

competitive_landscape.title: Saddle-to-Saddle Dynamics in Deep Linear Networks: Small Initialization Training, Symmetry, and Sparsity
competitive_landscape.difference: Jacot et al. formulate saddle-to-saddle rank growth for deep linear networks, prove the first transition, and analyze initialization-width phase structure. AGF provides an explicit alternating ansatz and several two-layer reductions, but does not extend its convergence proof to deep linear networks or settle the earlier full-path conjecture.

competitive_landscape.title: SGD learning on neural networks: leap complexity and saddle-to-saddle dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Abbe et al. derive saddle-to-saddle support learning and dimension-dependent SGD time complexity for hierarchical low-dimensional targets, explicitly going beyond mean-field and gradient-flow approximations. AGF covers a broader menu of toy architectures through one mechanism and predicts plateau magnitudes/times, but lacks comparable stochastic, sample-complexity, and computational-complexity guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Dynamics of In-Context Learning in Linear Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. directly reduce separate-key/query linear-attention training to scalar ODEs and show sequential principal-component regression, while also contrasting a merged parametrization with one abrupt transition. AGF recasts the separate-parametrization result as utility/cost alternation and supplies a generic lower-bound template, but its attention application is a recovery of that prior analysis rather than a new exact attention trajectory.

competitive_landscape.title: The Optimization Landscape of SGD Across the Feature Learning Strength
competitive_landscape.relationship: empirical competing account of plateaus and staircase regimes
competitive_landscape.difference: Atanasov et al. map staircase behavior across feature-strength and learning-rate scalings in multiple models and datasets, including an ultra-rich regime and time-reparameterized trajectories. AGF offers a sharper mechanistic decomposition for selected two-layer systems, but its empirical breadth is smaller and it does not explain the full feature-strength phase diagram.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Mechanism and Dynamics of Modular Addition: Fourier Features, Lottery Ticket, and Grokking
competitive_landscape.difference: He et al. give a later two-layer modular-addition account based on per-neuron frequency competition, phase symmetry, frequency diversification, a lottery-ticket mechanism, and weight-decay-driven grokking stages. This overlaps the claim of a complete dynamics theory and covers random initialization and collective solution formation, while AGF's distinctive result is ordered residual deflation for generalized cyclic encodings under grouped-alignment assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent in the Saddle-to-Saddle Regime of Deep Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Corlouer et al. model anisotropic state-dependent SGD noise in deep linear saddle-to-saddle training and derive per-mode stochastic differential equations plus stationary distributions under alignment and balance. AGF gives a broader deterministic feature-selection vocabulary but does not model stochastic diffusion, label noise, or deep networks.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: AGF is a unified algorithmic framework that predicts feature identity, order, timing, and loss drops across two-layer architectures and provides the first complete account of Fourier-feature training dynamics for modular addition.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper genuinely supplies a reusable dormant-utility/active-cost formalism, proves exact convergence in diagonal linear networks, makes prior low-rank and linear-attention results instances of the same template, and derives new harmonic utility and residual-deflation results for generalized cyclic encodings. Yet most component phenomena have direct predecessors, the general convergence and noncommuting linear claims remain open, and the modular cost trajectory uses grouped activation and harmonic-preservation assumptions; a 2026 modular-addition paper now supplies a different comprehensive dynamics account.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest defensible novelty as of 2026-08-23 is the cross-architecture abstraction plus the particular generalized-modular Fourier deflation analysis, not a general theorem of feature learning or an unconditional complete characterization of modular-addition training. AGF is valuable as a falsifiable ansatz and organizing language whose exactness is currently proved in one core setting and selectively derived in structured others.

reviewer_notes: Read against the indexed 40-page NeurIPS/arXiv source, including all proof appendices. The review distinguishes exact theorem, conjecture, lower bound, assumption, and qualitative plot. The odd-p versus p=20 audit follows the paper's own proof step that uses 2ξ and 4ξ nonresonance; it does not assert that the displayed experiment is invalid, only that it is outside the stated theorem assumptions. Competitor titles, versions, and relationships were checked on primary arXiv records on 2026-08-23. This primary pass does not independently reproduce code or constitute the required second-review verification.
